papers.title: Hantavirus infections in Southeastern Europe - Epidemiology, outbreak dynamics, and One Health preparedness: A narrative review.
papers.abstract: Human-pathogenic orthohantaviruses are significant rodent-borne zoonotic pathogens in Europe. Southeastern Europe (SEE) is a distinct endemic region where Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV) and Puumala virus (PUUV) co-circulate, causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) of varying severity. This narrative review synthesizes the epidemiology, transmission dynamics, clinical characteristics, ecological drivers, and public health challenges of hantavirus infections across SEE, identifying priorities for regional preparedness. We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science from their inception through June 2026, supplementing with reference screening. Regional epidemiological patterns were assessed descriptively using national surveillance data, European surveillance reports, published studies, and available population-based incidence estimates. Long-term surveillance reveals persistent endemic transmission with significant geographic and interannual heterogeneity. Slovenia and Croatia exhibit the highest cumulative burden and most pronounced periods of increased HFRS activity. Several years-2008, 2012, 2014, 2017, 2019, 2021, and 2023-showed partially synchronized increases across multiple neighboring countries. These patterns align with shared ecological influences, including rodent population fluctuations, mast-seeding events, and climatic variability. However, local ecology, human exposure, and differences in surveillance capacity modify their magnitude. The coexistence of generally milder PUUV-associated disease and more severe DOBV-associated HFRS further distinguishes SEE's clinical landscape. Therefore, hantavirus epidemiology in SEE is best understood as an interconnected regional ecological system. Integrated human, animal, environmental, and genomic surveillance within a coordinated One Health framework is crucial for improving outbreak prediction, cross-border preparedness, and future disease control.

Keywords: Orthohantavirus, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, Dobrava– Belgrade virus, Puumala virus, Southeastern Europe, zoonoses, One Health approach. 4 INTRODUCTION Human-pathogenic orthohantaviruses (family Hantaviridae) are among the most important rodent-borne zoonotic viruses worldwide and are responsible for the clinical syndromes collectively referred to as hantavirus disease [1,2]. Throughout this review, the term orthohantavirus is used when referring to the virus taxonomy, whereas hantavirus disease and related clinical terminology are retained for consistency with established medical nomenclature. In Eurasia, hantavirus infections primarily manifest as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), whereas in the Americas they cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS, also known as HPS) [3,4]. Their public health significance extends beyond their clinical impact and reflects their remarkable ability to persist silently within particular small-mammal reservoir hosts, amplify under favorable ecological conditions, and periodically emerge as geographically focal outbreaks in human populations [5–7]. Consequently, hantavirus disease represents a paradigmatic example of a zoonotic pathogen shaped by complex interactions among viral biology, reservoir ecology, land use, and climatic conditions [6–8]. In Europe, the epidemiological and public-health landscape is dominated by Old World orthohantaviruses, particularly Puumala virus (PUUV) and Dobrava–Belgrade virus (DOBV), that vary in reservoir associations, ecological niches, geographical distribution, and typical disease severity, yet together account for the majority of the regional HFRS burden [4,9,10]. Southeastern Europe (SEE) occupies a unique position within the European orthohantavirus landscape and cannot be viewed merely as a southern extension of the PUUV-dominated ecosystems of Central and Northern Europe. Rather it represents one of the few European macro-regions where highly pathogenic DOBV lineages and less virulent PUUV strains coexist in shared ecological and clinical space, thereby contributing to a heterogeneous regional risk signature that cannot be understood with respect to northern-European nephropathia epidemica models alone [4,9]. As no single definition of SEE exists, for the purposes of this review the region comprises Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH), Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Romania, Serbia, and Slovenia. SEE countries have played an important role in hantavirus research, as DOBV was first identified in the former Yugoslavia [10]. The region remains characterized by endemic circulation of orthohantaviruses in both human populations and rodent reservoirs, with marked 5 geographic heterogeneity and localized transmission foci. Thus, human infections and evidence of viral circulation have been documented across all countries included in the study [11–16] . Although clinical reporting remains limited in some parts of the region, there is evidence of ongoing viral circulation throughout. Renewed interest in hantavirus disease across SEE has been driven by climatic variability, changing reservoir ecology, land-use change, and evolving human exposure patterns, all of which contribute to dynamic transmission risk across the region [5,17–19]. Therefore, hantavirus disease in SEE should be interpreted not as a static endemicity problem, but as a dynamic interface between reservoir ecology, environmental change, and human activities. Accordingly, this review synthesizes current evidence on hantavirus epidemiology, clinical characteristics, ecological drivers, and public health challenges across SEE, with particular emphasis on regional outbreak patterns and cross-border epidemiological dynamics. Search strategy and data sources This review was based on a structured search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science to identify literature relevant to orthohantavirus disease in Southeastern Europe. Searches covered publications available from database inception until June 2026 and combined terms including “hantavirus”, “orthohantavirus”, “hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome”, “Southeastern Europe”, “Balkans”, and the names of individual countries within the study region. Additional relevant publications were identified through manual screening of reference lists of eligible articles. The review focuses on the epidemiology, clinical manifestations, transmission dynamics, and public health implications of human hantavirus infections in Southeastern Europe. As this is a narrative review, studies were selected according to their relevance to the scope of the manuscript rather than through formal systematic-review methodology. The epidemiological data presented in Table 2 were compiled from multiple complementary sources, including annual surveillance reports of the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), official national public health reports, and country-specific datasets provided or verified by collaborating public health experts where available. Given the heterogeneity of surveillance systems, reporting practices, and laboratory confirmation procedures across countries, epidemiological 6 data were interpreted descriptively. The primary data source for each country is summarized in Table S1. For countries with ECDC-derived data, EU-level surveillance through TESSy is available from 2008 onward; therefore, our comparative analysis covers 2008–2024, while earlier years are reported as N/A. Heyman et al. independently documented laboratory-diagnosed hantavirus infections in Greece, Slovenia, Romania, and Bulgaria during 2005–2007 [20]. We cite these findings as evidence of earlier hantavirus activity, but do not combine them with the ECDC or national data because the two sources are based on different surveillance approaches. Annual incidence rates were calculated as: Incidence (per 100,000 population) = (annual number of reported HFRS cases / corresponding annual mid-year population estimate) × 100,000. Annual country-specific mid-year population estimates were obtained from the World Bank DataBank, World Development Indicators (indicator SP.POP.TOTL) and matched to the corresponding surveillance year for each country. World Bank data were accessed on July 9 2026 [21]. Epidemiology of hantavirus infections in Southeastern Europe HFRS has been recognized in SEE for more than half a century, and the region remains a well-established endemic region characterized by sporadic cases each year punctuated by periodic epidemics [9]. A distinct north-south gradient is evident across the region, with PUUV being relatively more common in the northern part of the region, and DOBV predominating in the southern Balkans [9,22]. SEE is also the cradle of DOBV taxonomy: the prototype Dobrava strain was recovered from yellow- necked mouse (A. flavicollis) in Slovenia, while Belgrade virus was isolated from a fatal HFRS case in Serbia, with both subsequently confirmed as genetically identical [10,23]. DOBV and PUUV co-circulate widely across the Balkans, with generally moderate reported regional incidence but subject to marked interannual variability driven by multi-annual rodent population cycles [19]. Outbreaks typically follow mast-seeding events and favorable climatic conditions, including winters that enhance rodent survival and reproduction [4,6,7]. 7 Subclinical infections are common, with estimated subclinical-to-clinical ratios ranging from 5:1 to 20:1, resulting in substantial under-ascertainment, particularly of mild PUUV-associated disease [19,24,25]. Seroepidemiological surveys indicate substantial background exposure with a clear geographic gradient: overall seroprevalence has been estimated at approximately 6% in BiH, approximately 4% in Greece (range 0 to 14% by county), 3.1% in Bulgaria, 1.7% in Slovenia, and 1.6% in Croatia, with higher rates reported among occupationally exposed populations and local foci [9,14,25–29]. Evidence of viral circulation has been documented across the SEE region, although the dominant virus and disease burden vary according to local ecology, rodent-host distribution, and surveillance intensity (Table 1). Albania and Kosovo were not included in the comparative surveillance analysis presented in Table 2 because continuous annual surveillance data were not publicly available for inclusion; therefore, the information presented for these countries is based primarily on the available published evidence. BiH has been a major endemic focus of hantavirus infections in Europe for more than 50 years. Outbreaks have been documented since 1967, with large epidemics in the former Yugoslavia during 1986-1987 and 1989, involving more than 1,000 reported cases, and further outbreaks in 1995 and 2002, the latter implicating PUUV, DOBV and untyped serotypes [30–34] . Following the 2002 epidemic, hantavirus infections continued to occur regularly in BiH, with at least one confirmed case reported annually between 2005 and 2024 (Table 2). Although annual case numbers were generally low, pronounced peaks were observed in 2014, 2017, and 2021, supporting the persistence of endemic circulation with periodic outbreaks. While the majority of reported cases originate from central and northeastern Bosnia, the distribution of rodent reservoirs and serological evidence of exposure indicate that hantavirus circulation extends beyond these recognized endemic foci [27,35]. Consequently, the geographic distribution of infection may be broader than that indicated by routine surveillance data. In Croatia, both DOBV and PUUV contribute to disease burden, with a notable military outbreak in 1995, and large epidemics in 2002, 2012, 2014, 2017, and 2021. Notably, the 2012 Medvednica outbreak was linked to exceptionally high PUUV infection rates in bank voles, while the 2017 (≈389 notified cases) and 2021 (≈334 8 cases) outbreaks were the largest on record and extended into Adriatic-coastal and other areas previously considered non-endemic [18,36,37]. Serbia has reported HFRS since 1961, with Belgrade virus characterized during a 1989 epidemic and subsequent molecular confirmation of DOBV circulation foci in western and central regions [10,38,39] . Serbian national surveillance demonstrates persistent endemic HFRS activity, with generally low annual incidence punctuated by occasional increases in reported cases. In Greece, serological evidence dates to 1981, with 0–4 HFRS cases reported annually in recent years and an estimated case-fatality of approximately 9% among hospitalized patients, a figure derived from severely ill cases and therefore an overestimate of the overall rate [14,40]. DOBV (genotype Dobrava, hosted by A. flavicollis) predominates, with 80% of all cases occurring in endemic foci in the Rhodope and Pindos mountains near the northern borders and no cases reported from southern Greece or the islands, whereas PUUV is also endemic but accounts for far fewer recognized cases [10,14] . Despite relatively low annual notification rates, the persistence of endemic foci and serological evidence of exposure indicate continuous viral circulation, emphasizing the importance of maintaining surveillance in northern Greece. Bulgaria has recorded HFRS since the 1950s, mainly across the Rila-Pirin-Rodopi massifs of the southwest, where phylogenetically related DOBV strains circulate in Apodemus mice, confirming local rodent reservoirs [9,10,16]. Although reported incidence has remained consistently low, the continued detection of DOBV in both rodents and human cases supports persistent endemic transmission rather than sporadic viral introduction. Albania likewise has confirmed hantavirus circulation through genetic detection in rodent hosts [12,41–43], while Kosovo reports severe DOBV-associated HFRS, with documented population seroconversion in endemic zones and severe sporadic cases [15,44,45]. Slovenia represents one of the most affected countries in SEE, experiencing recurrent large-scale outbreaks and the highest incidence rates recorded in the region, particularly during 2012, 2019, and 2021. In contrast, Montenegro reports relatively few cases but periodically reaches among the highest annual incidence rates in SEE 9 owing to its small population size, illustrating the importance of interpreting incidence alongside absolute case numbers [46] . North Macedonia has reported only sporadic cases in recent years, although limited surveillance coverage makes it difficult to determine the true extent of endemic circulation [11]. Hantavirus infections in Romania remain rare but endemic, with sporadic cases reported over the past two decades, primarily caused by DOBV [4,13] . Despite the low number of reported cases, increasing recognition through improved diagnostics and surveillance suggests that hantavirus infections may be more widespread than previously appreciated. The comparative analysis of 20-year surveillance data presented in Table 2, based on long-term national surveillance data and complemented by ECDC surveillance reports and published national epidemiological studies, further illustrates the heterogeneous yet interconnected epidemiological landscape of hantavirus infections in SEE. DOI: https://doi.org/10.17305/bb.2026.14790 3 ABSTRACT Human-pathogenic orthohantaviruses are significant rodent-borne zoonotic pathogens in Europe. Southeastern Europe (SEE) is a distinct endemic region where Dobrava- Belgrade virus (DOBV) and Puumala virus (PUUV) co-circulate, causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) of varying severity. This narrative review synthesizes the epidemiology, transmission dynamics, clinical characteristics, ecological drivers, and public health challenges of hantavirus infections across SEE, identifying priorities for regional preparedness. We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science from their inception through June 2026, supplementing with reference screening. Regional epidemiological patterns were assessed descriptively using national surveillance data, European surveillance reports, published studies, and available population-based incidence estimates. Long-term surveillance reveals persistent endemic transmission with significant geographic and interannual heterogeneity. Slovenia and Croatia exhibit the highest cumulative burden and most pronounced periods of increased HFRS activity. Several years—2008, 2012, 2014, 2017, 2019, 2021, and 2023—showed partially synchronized increases across multiple neighboring countries. These patterns align with shared ecological influences, including rodent population fluctuations, mast-seeding events, and climatic variability. However, local ecology, human exposure, and differences in surveillance capacity modify their magnitude. The coexistence of generally milder PUUV-associated disease and more severe DOBV-associated HFRS further distinguishes SEE's clinical landscape. Therefore, hantavirus epidemiology in SEE is best understood as an interconnected regional ecological system. Integrated human, animal, environmental, and genomic surveillance within a coordinated One Health framework is crucial for improving outbreak prediction, cross-border preparedness, and future disease control. Keywords: Orthohantavirus, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, Dobrava– Belgrade virus, Puumala virus, Southeastern Europe, zoonoses, One Health approach. 4 INTRODUCTION Human-pathogenic orthohantaviruses (family Hantaviridae) are among the most important rodent-borne zoonotic viruses worldwide and are responsible for the clinical syndromes collectively referred to as hantavirus disease [1,2]. Throughout this review, the term orthohantavirus is used when referring to the virus taxonomy, whereas hantavirus disease and related clinical terminology are retained for consistency with established medical nomenclature. In Eurasia, hantavirus infections primarily manifest as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), whereas in the Americas they cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS, also known as HPS) [3,4]. Their public health significance extends beyond their clinical impact and reflects their remarkable ability to persist silently within particular small-mammal reservoir hosts, amplify under favorable ecological conditions, and periodically emerge as geographically focal outbreaks in human populations [5–7]. Consequently, hantavirus disease represents a paradigmatic example of a zoonotic pathogen shaped by complex interactions among viral biology, reservoir ecology, land use, and climatic conditions [6–8]. In Europe, the epidemiological and public-health landscape is dominated by Old World orthohantaviruses, particularly Puumala virus (PUUV) and Dobrava–Belgrade virus (DOBV), that vary in reservoir associations, ecological niches, geographical distribution, and typical disease severity, yet together account for the majority of the regional HFRS burden [4,9,10]. Southeastern Europe (SEE) occupies a unique position within the European orthohantavirus landscape and cannot be viewed merely as a southern extension of the PUUV-dominated ecosystems of Central and Northern Europe. Rather it represents one of the few European macro-regions where highly pathogenic DOBV lineages and less virulent PUUV strains coexist in shared ecological and clinical space, thereby contributing to a heterogeneous regional risk signature that cannot be understood with respect to northern-European nephropathia epidemica models alone [4,9]. As no single definition of SEE exists, for the purposes of this review the region comprises Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH), Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Romania, Serbia, and Slovenia. SEE countries have played an important role in hantavirus research, as DOBV was first identified in the former Yugoslavia [10]. The region remains characterized by endemic circulation of orthohantaviruses in both human populations and rodent reservoirs, with marked 5 geographic heterogeneity and localized transmission foci. Thus, human infections and evidence of viral circulation have been documented across all countries included in the study [11–16] . Although clinical reporting remains limited in some parts of the region, there is evidence of ongoing viral circulation throughout. full_text_sections.full_text: RAZAFINDRALAMBO Nadia Kaloina ARENAVIRUS ET HANTAVIRUS CHEZ LES PETITS MAMMIFERES SAUVAGES TERRESTRES DE MADAGASCAR IDENTIFIES PAR RT-PCR Thèse de Doctorat en Médecine Vétérinaire UNIVERSITE D’ANTANANARIVO FACULTE DE MEDECINE DEPARTEMENT D’ENSEINGNEMENT DES SCIENCES ET DE MEDECINE VETERINAIRES ANNEE : 2011 N° :064 ARENAVIRUS ET HANTAVIRUS CHEZ LES PETITS MAMMIFERES SAUVAGES TERRESTRES DE MADAGASCAR IDENTIFIES PAR RT-PCR THESE Présentée et soutenue publiquement le 16 septembre 2011 à Antananarivo par Mademoiselle RAZAFINDRALAMBO Nadia Kaloina Née le 30 Septembre 1988 à Soavinandriana Antananarivo Pour obtenir le grade de << DOCTEUR EN MEDECINE VETERINAIRE >> (Diplôme d’Etat) Directeur de thèse : Professeur RASAMINDRAKOTROKA Andry MEMBRES DU JURY Président : Professeur RASAMINDRAKOTROKA Andry Juges : Professeur RANDRIANJAFISAMINDRAKOTROKA Nantenaina Soa Professeur RAKOTOZANDRINDRAINY Raphaël Rapporteur : Dr RASOLOFO RAZANAMPARANY Voahangy DEDICACE Je dédie cette thèse : A DIEU Tout Puissant : qui m’a donné la vie et m’a accordé la chance de faire cette thèse. Qu’Il nous accorde sa grâce. « Je t’instruirai et te montrerai la voie que tu dois suivre ; Je te conseillerai, J’aurai le regard sur toi » Psaumes 328 A mes parents : pour tant d’année de sacrifice vos encouragements, votre soutien moral et matériel et votre optimisme dans la vie, m’ont marqué, des qualités qui ont fait de vous des parents exemplaires. Je n’ai pas le mot pour dire ce que je ressens. Veuillez trouvez dans cet humble ouvrage les récompenses de vos efforts. Ce travail est le modeste témoignage de toute mon affection et mon profond respect. Qu’il soit le témoin de mon immense reconnaissance. Que Dieu le Tout Puissant vous garde. Amen A mes sœurs : pour leur support et encouragement, recevez ma tendre affection. Que l’esprit de fraternité nous anime pour toujours. A mes oncles et mes tantes paternels et maternels, à toutes les familles : Je n’ai rien à vous offrir en guise de récompenses. Que la bénédiction de Dieu vous accompagne durant toute votre vie pour qu’Il vous donne mille fois plus que ce que vous avez donné. A mes amis A tous ceux qui ont contribué de loin ou de près à la réalisation de ce travail. A NOTRE MAITRE DIRECTEUR ET PRESIDENT DE THESE Monsieur le Docteur RASAMINDRAKOTROKA Andry Professeur Titulaire d’Enseignement Supérieur et de la Recherche en Immunologie à la Faculté de Médecine d’Antananarivo. « Vous avez accepté de diriger cette thèse et vous avez accueilli sans reserve et avec bienveillance malgré vos incompréhensibles obligations. Vous nous faites aussi l’honneur d’accepter de présider notre thèse. Veuillez trouver à travers ce travail l’expression de notre profonde gratitude » A NOS MAITRES ET HONORABLES JUGES DE THESE Monsieur le Docteur RANDRIANJAFISAMINDRAKOTROKA Nantenaina Soa Professeur Titulaire d’Enseignement Supérieur et de la Recherche en Anatomie Pathologique à la Faculté de Médecine d’Antananarivo. Monsieur le Docteur RAKOTOZANDRINDRAINY Raphaël Professeur Spécialiste en Microbiologie et Parasitologie à l’Ecole Supérieure des Sciences Agronomiques. Enseignant à la Faculté de Médecine d’Antananarivo et au Département d’Enseignement des Sciences et de Médecine Vétérinaires. Nous vous remercions d’avoir accepté de juger ce travail, un peu éloigné de vos préoccupations habituelles. Veuillez bien trouver ici le témoignage de notre respectueuse reconnaissance. A NOTRE RAPPORTEUR DE THESE : Madame le Docteur RASOLOFO RAZANAMPARANY Voahangy Chef de l’Unité de Mycobactéries à l’Institut Pasteur de Madagascar Vous avez bien voulu nous aider dans l’élaboration de ce travail malgré vos lourdes préoccupations. Ce travail que vous nous avez confié est aussi le fruit de votre immense expérience. Nous vous exprimons notre profonde reconnaissance. A NOTRE MAITRE ET DOYEN DE LA FACULTE DE MEDECINE D’ANTANANARIVO Monsieur le Professeur RAPELANORO RABENJA Fahafahantsoa Veuillez recevoir l’expression de notre haute considération. A MES ENCADREURS Monsieur le Docteur Jean-Marc REYNES Monsieur le Docteur Jean-Michel HERAUD Sincères remerciements. A TOUS NOS MAITRES ET PROFESSEURS DE LA FACULTE DE MEDECINE D’ANTANANARIVO - DEPARTEMENT D’ENSEIGNEMENT DES SCIENCES ET DE MEDECINE VETERINAIRES. Notre reconnaissance pour tous les enseignements que vous nous avez prodigués. A TOUT LE PERSONNEL ADMINISTRATIF ET TECHNIQUE DE LA FACULTE DE MEDECINE D’ANTANANARIVO. Merci infiniment. papers.title: Integrated Analysis of Human Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome Cases and Rodent Hantavirus Surveillance in Zhejiang Province, China, 2025
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Seoul orthohantavirus (SEOV) and Hantaan orthohantavirus (HTNV), remains a neglected rodent-borne zoonosis with persistent residual spillover risk in low-incidence regions of China. This study assessed human HFRS occurrence and small-mammal hantavirus surveillance signals in small-mammal hosts across Zhejiang Province, China, in 2025. Reported human cases were obtained from the National Notifiable Disease Surveillance System, and animal host surveillance was conducted at five designated monitoring sites. A total of 107 HFRS cases were reported, occurring year-round with peaks in June and December and showing spatial heterogeneity, presenting a predominance of males, adults aged ≥40 years, and farmers. Animal host surveillance captured 617 small mammals (566 rodents and 51 shrews) from 15,457 valid trap-nights, with Apodemus agrarius (30.31%) and Rattus norvegicus (29.98%) as the dominant species. Sixteen animals were positive for hantavirus RNA and/or antibody, including 12 for hantavirus RNA and 6 antibody-positive animals; two were positive for both markers. Positive animals were detected in multiple species, including Niviventer confucianus, R. norvegicus, Rattus losea, A. agrarius, Suncus murinus, and Rattus tanezumi. Human incidence, small-mammal density, host species composition, and hantavirus-positive rates were not fully concordant across surveillance sites. Our findings reveal sustained cryptic orthohantavirus circulation in low-endemic Zhejiang, highlighting that integrated human-reservoir One Health surveillance is indispensable for precise spillover risk prediction and targeted zoonotic disease intervention.

analysis.methods: Human HFRS cases from the National Notifiable Disease Surveillance System were combined with small‑mammal hantavirus surveillance at five sites in Zhejiang Province in 2025, capturing 617 rodents and shrews over 15,457 trap‑nights.
analysis.results: 107 HFRS cases occurred year‑round with peaks in June and December, mainly among male farmers aged ≥40 years; 16 of the captured mammals (including Apodemus agrarius, Rattus norvegicus and other species) were hantavirus RNA‑ and/or antibody‑positive (12 RNA‑positive, 6 antibody‑positive, 2 with both), and human incidence did not fully match small‑mammal density or positive‑rate patterns across sites.
analysis.contribution: The study reveals sustained cryptic orthohantavirus circulation in a low‑endemic area and highlights the need for integrated One Health surveillance to improve spillover risk prediction and guide targeted interventions.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by SEOV and HTNV, is a neglected rodent‑borne zoonosis with persistent spillover risk in low‑incidence China. Methods: Human HFRS cases from the national surveillance system were integrated with small‑mammal hantavirus surveillance at five Zhejiang sites in 2025, capturing 617 rodents/shrews over 15,457 trap‑nights. Results: 107 cases occurred year‑round, peaking in June and December, mainly male farmers ≥40 years; 16 mammals (including A. agrarius, R. norvegicus) were hantavirus RNA‑/antibody‑positive (12 RNA, 6 antibody, 2 both), and human incidence did not fully align with host density or positivity rates. Contribution: Findings show sustained cryptic orthohantavirus circulation and underscore the necessity of integrated One Health surveillance for accurate spillover risk prediction and targeted control. Limitations: Only an abstract is provided, so detailed methods and full results are not reported.

papers.title_zh: 中国浙江省2025年人类肾综合征出血热病例与啮齿动物汉坦病毒监测的综合分析

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(HFRS),由首尔病毒(SEOV)和汉滩病毒(HTNV)引起,是一种被忽视的啮齿动物源人畜共患病,在中国低发地区仍存在持续的跨种传播风险。
analysis_zh.methods: 将国家法定传染病监测系统的人类HFRS病例与2025年浙江省五个地点的小型哺乳动物汉坦病毒监测相结合,共捕获617只啮齿动物和鼩鼱,累计捕鼠夜数为15,457。
analysis_zh.results: 全年共出现107例HFRS病例,峰值出现在6月和12月,主要集中在≥40岁的男性农民;捕获的哺乳动物中有16例(包括田鼠Apodemus agrarius、家鼠Rattus norvegicus等)检测到汉坦病毒 RNA和/或抗体阳性(12例RNA阳性,6例抗体阳性,2例两者皆阳),且各地区的人类发病率并未完全对应小型哺乳动物密度或阳性率的分布模式。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究揭示了低流行区持续的隐匿正汉坦病毒循环,强调需要开展综合One Health监测,以提升跨种传播风险预测并指导有针对性的干预措施。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要,未报告详细的方法学、统计分析和完整结果。

papers.title: The necessity of adding Hantavirus infection to the differential diagnosis of Iran syndromic surveillance
papers.abstract: Iran's syndromic surveillance system is continuously monitoring emerging infectious diseases.Given the serological and molecular evidence of hantavirus circulation in rodent reservoirs and the human population of the country, strengthening diagnostic approaches in this system is important.In addition to presenting with manifestations such as renal and respiratory syndromes, hantavirus requires a distinct place in the differential diagnosis protocols of acute respiratory and influenza-like infections.Utilizing existing laboratory capacities, along with ongoing training for early identification of suspicious cases, can significantly strengthen the current surveillance system in managing possible outbreaks and responding to these potential threats
papers.journal: Journal of Health Research and Development

مولکول ی از گردش هانتاو روس ی در مخازن جوندگان و جمع تی انسان ی کشور، تقو تی ی رو کردها ی تشخ یصی نی در ا نظام حائز اهم تی است. هانتاو روس ی عالوه بر ا نی که م ی تواند با تظاهرات ی ری نظ سندرم ی ها یوی کل و تنفس ی بروز کند، ن ی ازمند ی گاه ی جا متما زی در پروتکل ی ها تشخ صی افتراق ی عفونت ی ها حاد تنفس ی و شبه آنفلوآنزا است. بهره یریگ از ظرف ی ها تی آزما ی شگاه ی موجود، در کنار آموزش مداوم برا ی شناسا یی زودهنگام موارد مشکوک، م ی تواند نظام مرا قبت ی فعل را در مد تیری ان ی طغ ی ها احتمال ی و پاسخ به ا ین تهد دات ی بالقوه به طور چشمگ یری تی تقو دی نما. واژه های کلیدی :هانتاو ی،روس نظام مراقبت، روس ی در تشخ ی ها صی افتراق ی 3 احمدی وهمکاران jhrd.trjums.ac.ir مقدمه عفونت هانتاو روس ی (Hantavirus) یکی از مسائل مهمّ روز در حوزه ی بهداشت عموم ی (است1). جد نی دتر ی موارد گزارش ابتال به هانتاو روس ی در کشت ی کروز در ارد ی بهشت 1405 از مبدأ آرژانت نی به اق انوس ی اطلس جنوب ی بود که توسّط سازمان بهداشت جهان ی (WHO) گزارش و پاسخ بهداشت ی من اسب با مشارکت کشورها ی مربوط داده شد. ا نی ی مار یب به طور عمده به دو شکل تب خونر یزی دهنده با سندرم کل یوی (HFRS) و سندرم قلب ی یویر (HCPS) ده ید یم شود(2). اول ین مورد هانتاو روس ی در ا ران ی سال1982 مشاهده شده و تاکنون شواهد سرم ی و مولکول ی حضور سو ی ها هی مختلف در ج تی مع انسان ی و جوندگان از10 استان ا ران ی(3 .) گزارش شده است کی متاآنال یز نشان داده است که ش وع ی ی سرم ی جهان نیا عفونت و روس ی ی در جمع تی انسان ی 93 /2درصد (است4 ). هر چند با توجه به و ی ها ی ژگ ی ی دم ی اپ ولوژ کی هانتاو روس ی،ها احتمال مشاهده ی ی مار یب به عنوان پاندم ی بعد ی ،کم است ان ی طغ ی ها ّی محل به خصوص در مناطق ی که م زبان ی مخزن وجود دارد، محتمل است. م زان ی کشندگ ی مورد بر اساس هی سو ی ها مختلف از1درصد تا5/ 44درصد (متفاوت است5 .) روس یو آندس (Andes) به دل لی تی قابل انتقال انسان به انسانّ اهمّتی ی اد یز دارد. نظام مراقبت سندرم یک 1 برخالف نظام مراقبت را ی،ج تا زمان تشخ صی قطع ی ی مار یب صبر نکرده و با نگاه به سندرم ی ها ینی بال ی سع دارد طغ ان ی ها ی مار یب شی را پ از تشخ صی قطع ی، شناسا یی و مد یریت کند. عفونت هانتاو روس ی نی از ا هی قض مستثن ی نبوده و با توجه به شواهد ی سرم و مولکول ی مشاهده شده در ا ی،ران الزم است عالوه بر سندرم تب و خون یزیر (6)، در فهرست تشخ ی ها صی افتراق ی سندرم ی ها ( تب و راش حاد7 ( )، شبه آنفلوآنزا8 ) و عفونت دی شد تنفّس ی (9) قرار گ رد ی. در حال حاضر، در کتاب راهنما ی نظام مراقبت سندرم ی،ک عفونت هانتاو روس ی فقط در فهرست تشخ ی ها صی افتراق ی سندرم تب و خون ریزی قرار دارد. قرار گرفتن عفونت هانتاو روس ی در فهرست تشخ ی ها صی افتراق ی ری سا سندرم ی ها فوق م ی تواند به شناسا یی زودهنگام ان ی طغ ی ها نیا عفونت کمک کند . البته در مورد سندرم تب و راش حاد، ا نی سندرم صرفا ً در سو یهی Puumala ده ید شده(است7) که به نظر نم ی رسد سوش را یجی ران ی در ا باشد؛ هرچند مورد آن در ا ران ی گزارش شده(است10 ). در موارد ان ی طغ با سندرم ی ها اشاره شده، الزم است در فرا ند ی بررس ی ان ی طغ (outbreak investigation) یکی از فرض ی ها هی ما ان ی طغ عفونت هانتاو روس ی باشد. در چن نی یطی شرا از ین به بررس ی ها ی مولکول ی و دق تر قی وجود خواهد داشت. با توجه به وجود آزما ی شگاه مرجع تب ی ها خونر یزی دهنده در انست تو ی پاستور ا ی،ران در صورت ارجاع مناسب، موارد جد دی ی مار یب تشخ صی ده دا خواهند شد(شکل1). با توجه به شواهد موجود ی مبن بر گردش هانتاو روس ی در مخازن جانور ی زی و ن ی اب ی رد آن در ج تی مع انسان ی یا،ران توجه نظام مند به ا ین عفونت در چارچوب برنامه ی ها مراقبت ی کشور از اهم تی یا ژه یو برخوردار است. در ا نی ی زم،نه الزم است تأک ید شود که نظام مراقبت یا،ران همانند ی رو کرد اتّخاذشده برا ی یی ها ی مار یب ری نظ تب خون ریزی دهنده ـ مه ی کر کنگو ( CCHF )، از تی ظرف الزم برا ی شناسا یی، گزارش ی ده ی فور موارد مشکوک، حساس ی ساز و آموزش کارکنان نظام بهداشت ی و درمان ی برخوردار است و توان یم نی از ا یز رساخت ها ی برا تی تقو توجه به هانتاو روس ی زین بهره گرفت. ازا نی،رو گنجاندن فعاالنه عفونت هانتاو روس ی در فهرست تشخ ی ها صی افتراق ی سندرم ی ها مرتبط و بازنگر ی ای تکم لی راهنماها ی ی مل مراقبت ب ها ی مار ی و پروتکل ی ها بررس ی ان ی طغ ی ها ینی بال، با اتکا به روش ی ها تشخ یصی مولکول ی، می تواند به شناسا یی به موقع موارد و پاسخ تر عی سر به ا نی تهد دی بالقوه کمک کند. بد یهی است تحقق مؤثر ا نی امر مستلزم آن است که فرا ند ی بازنگر ی و طرّاح ی اجزا ی مرتبط نظام مراقبت سندرم ی،ک با مشارکت صاحب نظران و بهره یریگ از ظرف ی ها تی موجود نظام سالمت .کشور انجام شود 1 (syndromic surveillance) ضرورت اضافه شدن عفونت هانتاو ی،ج تا زمان تشخ صی قطع ی ی مار یب صبر نکرده و با نگاه به سندرم ی ها ینی بال ی سع دارد طغ ان ی ها ی مار یب شی را پ از تشخ صی قطع ی، شناسا یی و مد یریت کند. عفونت هانتاو روس ی نی از ا هی قض مستثن ی تنفّس ی (9) قرار گ رد ی. در حال حاضر، در کتاب راهنما ی نظام مراقبت سندرم ی،ک عفونت هانتاو روس ی فقط در فهرست تشخ ی ها صی افتراق ی سندرم تب و خون ریزی قرار دارد. قرار گرفتن عفونت هانتاو روس ی در فهرست تشخ ی ها صی افتراق ی ری سا سندرم ی ها فوق م ی تواند به شناسا یی زودهنگام ان ی طغ ی ها نیا عفونت کمک کند . البته در مورد سندرم تب و راش حاد، ا نی سندرم صرفا ً در سو یهی Puumala ده ید شده(است7) که به نظر نم ی رسد سوش را یجی ران ی در ا باشد؛ هرچند مورد آن در ا ران ی گزارش شده(است10 ). در موارد ان ی طغ با سندرم ی ها اشاره شده، الزم است در فرا ند ی بررس ی ان ی طغ (outbreak investigation) یکی از فرض ی ها هی ما ان ی طغ عفونت هانتاو روس ی باشد. در چن نی یطی شرا از ین به بررس ی ها ی مولکول ی و دق تر قی وجود خواهد داشت. با توجه به وجود آزما ی شگاه مرجع تب ی ها خونر یزی دهنده در انست تو ی پاستور ا ی،ران papers.title: Cardiopulmonary Failure in Hantavirus Disease: Mechanisms, Recognition, and ECMO-Based Management.
papers.abstract: Background: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), also designated hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, is caused by New World hantaviruses, principally Sin Nombre virus in North America and Andes virus in South America. The syndrome is characterized by rapidly progressive noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and myocardial depression, with case fatality rates of 25% to 40%. A 2026 outbreak aboard an expedition cruise ship in the South Atlantic, comprising 13 cases and three deaths, confirmed that Andes virus can be transmitted between humans in a confined setting remote from the rodent reservoir. Methods: Virological, pathophysiological, clinical, and therapeutic aspects of HPS were reviewed, with particular emphasis on cardiopulmonary mechanisms. Sources were identified through PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, with priority given to original research articles, clinical series, and controlled trials published through 2025. Literature published in English and Spanish was included. Results: Pathogenic hantaviruses enter endothelial cells and platelets via αvβ3 integrins, disrupting the VEGF-VEGFR2 signaling axis and rendering endothelial cells hypersensitive to physiological VEGF concentrations. Expansion of CD8+ T cells and activated macrophages releases TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, and nitric oxide, amplifying microvascular permeability and contributing to myocardial depression. Autopsy studies demonstrate direct hantaviral myocarditis with viral antigen in cardiac endothelium and interstitial macrophages. Transpulmonary thermodilution confirms simultaneous hypovolemia, reduced global ejection fraction, and elevated extravascular lung water. Because the incubation period is long and the cardiopulmonary phase is substantially immune-mediated, seroconversion precedes rather than follows clinical deterioration, which preserves the diagnostic utility of IgM serology in a disease that can kill within 48 h. VA-ECMO initiated at the first signs of cardiopulmonary decompensation has reported survival rates approaching 80% in selected experienced centers. No antiviral has demonstrated efficacy in controlled trials during the cardiopulmonary phase, and no licensed vaccine exists. Conclusions: HPS produces a mixed shock state through increased microvascular permeability, T cell-mediated immunopathology, and direct myocarditis. Management follows a stepwise algorithm: suspected HPS triggers immediate complete blood count with peripheral blood smear and concurrent hantavirus IgM serology and RT-PCR, followed by ICU admission, conservative fluid resuscitation guided by transpulmonary thermodilution, and early contact with an ECMO-capable center at the first sign of rising lactate, falling cardiac index, refractory shock, arrhythmia, or rapid oxygenation failure.

A 2026 outbreak aboard an expedition cruise ship in the South Atlantic, comprising 13 cases and three deaths, confirmed that Andes virus can be transmitted between humans in a confined setting remote from the rodent reservoir. Methods: Virological, pathophysiological, clinical, and therapeutic aspects of HPS were reviewed, with particular emphasis on cardiopulmonary mechanisms. Sources were identified through PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, with priority given to original research articles, clinical series, and controlled trials published through 2025. Literature published in English and Spanish was included. Results: Pathogenic hantaviruses enter endothelial cells and platelets via αvβ3 integrins, disrupting the VEGF-VEGFR2 signaling axis and rendering endothelial cells hypersensitive to physiological VEGF concentrations. Expansion of CD8+ T cells and activated macrophages releases TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, and nitric oxide, amplifying microvascular permeability and contributing to myocardial depression. Autopsy studies demonstrate direct hantaviral myocarditis with viral antigen in cardiac endothelium and interstitial macrophages. Transpulmonary thermodilution confirms simultaneous hypovolemia, reduced global ejection fraction, and elevated extravascular lung water. Because the incubation period is long and the cardiopulmonary phase is substantially immune-mediated, seroconversion precedes rather than follows clinical deterioration, which preserves the diagnostic utility of IgM serology in a disease that can kill within 48 h. VA-ECMO initiated at the first signs of cardiopulmonary decompensation has reported survival rates approaching 80% in selected experienced centers. No antiviral has demonstrated efficacy in controlled trials during the cardiopulmonary phase, and no licensed vaccine exists. Conclusions: HPS produces a mixed shock state through increased microvascular permeability, T cell-mediated immunopathology, and direct myocarditis. Management follows a stepwise algorithm: suspected HPS triggers immediate complete blood count with peripheral blood smear and concurrent hantavirus IgM serology and RT-PCR, followed by ICU admission, conservative fluid resuscitation guided by transpulmonary thermodilution, and early contact with an ECMO-capable center at the first sign of rising lactate, falling cardiac index, refractory shock, arrhythmia, or rapid oxygenation failure.

analysis.background: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), caused by New World hantaviruses such as Sin Nombre and Andes virus, remains a high‑mortality disease prompting review of its cardiopulmonary failure mechanisms and management.
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on endothelial entry via αvβ3 integrins, immune‑mediated microvascular leak, direct myocarditis, and the role of early VA‑ECMO support in severe cases.
analysis.current_state: Evidence shows that endothelial disruption and CD8⁺ T‑cell activation drive pulmonary edema and myocardial depression, while early VA‑ECMO can achieve ~80% survival in experienced centers; no antiviral or licensed vaccine has proven effective.
analysis.gaps: There are no controlled‑trial data for antivirals, limited information on ECMO outcomes outside specialist centers, and sparse understanding of human‑to‑human transmission dynamics.
analysis.future_research: Randomized trials of candidate antivirals or immunomodulators, multicenter ECMO outcome registries, and studies of transmission risk in confined settings are needed to improve HPS treatment and prevention.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HPS caused by New World hantaviruses has high fatality, driving review of its cardiopulmonary failure. Main directions: The article examines endothelial entry, immune‑mediated leak, myocarditis, and early VA‑ECMO use. Current state: Endothelial disruption and T‑cell activation underlie disease; early ECMO yields ~80% survival in expert centers, but no effective antiviral or vaccine exists. Gaps: Lack of antiviral trial data, limited ECMO outcome data beyond specialist sites, and unclear human‑to‑human transmission. Future research: Conduct antiviral/immunomodulator trials, establish multicenter ECMO registries, and investigate transmission in confined environments.

papers.title: Hantavirus: A focused review for the emergency medicine clinician.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Andes virus (ANDV), a form of hantavirus, is a potentially fatal disease with several cases recently reported aboard an expedition cruise ship in April and May 2026. OBJECTIVE: This focused narrative review provides a focused overview of the epidemiology, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and management of hantavirus infection, including ANDV, for the emergency clinician. DISCUSSION: Human infections with hantavirus primarily occur through contact with aerosolized particles of saliva, feces, or urine of infected rodents or through touching contaminated surfaces. A recent outbreak of ANDV has demonstrated human-to-human transmission in the setting of close, prolonged contact. The incubation period ranges between 4 and 42 days. As hantaviruses target the endothelium of capillaries and small vessels, patients may develop hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, predominantly associated with hantaviruses found in Europe and Asia or hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, mainly associated with hantaviruses in the Americas. Both hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus with pulmonary syndrome present initially with a non-specific viral prodrome (e.g., fever, chills, malaise, myalgias). Following this prodrome, patients with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome can demonstrate coagulation abnormalities and change in urine output with renal dysfunction, while hantavirus with pulmonary syndrome presents with cardiopulmonary symptoms with cough, dyspnea, tachycardia, and hypotension that may progress to respiratory failure and cardiogenic shock. Diagnosis incorporates ELISA assay to detect IgG and IgM antibodies. Patients with concern for ANDV should be isolated in a private room (preferably a negative pressure room). Airborne and contact precautions are recommended; strategies similar to those employed for managing patients with viral hemorrhagic fever may be considered. Treatment is primarily supportive, including resuscitation with intravenous fluids and vasopressors, respiratory support (e.g., supplemental oxygen, noninvasive ventilation, endotracheal intubation), antipyretics and analgesics, and hemorrhage control as needed. Mechanical ventilation, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and hemodialysis may be necessary. CONCLUSION: Hantavirus may initially present with a non-specific viral prodrome, but travel and social history should prompt greater diagnostic suspicion. Patients are managed similarly to those with other viral hemorrhagic fevers.

Objective This focused narrative review provides a focused overview of the epidemiology, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and management of hantavirus infection, including ANDV, for the emergency clinician. Discussion Human infections with hantavirus primarily occur through contact with aerosolized particles of saliva, feces, or urine of infected rodents or through touching contaminated surfaces. A recent outbreak of ANDV has demonstrated human-to-human transmission in the setting of close, prolonged contact. The incubation period ranges between 4 and 42 days. As hantaviruses target the endothelium of capillaries and small vessels, patients may develop hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, predominantly associated with hantaviruses found in Europe and Asia or hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, mainly associated with hantaviruses in the Americas. Both hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus with pulmonary syndrome present initially with a non-specific viral prodrome (e.g., fever, chills, malaise, myalgias). Following this prodrome, patients with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome can demonstrate coagulation abnormalities and change in urine output with renal dysfunction, while hantavirus with pulmonary syndrome presents with cardiopulmonary symptoms with cough, dyspnea, tachycardia, and hypotension that may progress to respiratory failure and cardiogenic shock. Diagnosis incorporates ELISA assay to detect IgG and IgM antibodies. Patients with concern for ANDV should be isolated in a private room (preferably a negative pressure room). Airborne and contact precautions are recommended; strategies similar to those employed for managing patients with viral hemorrhagic fever may be considered. Treatment is primarily supportive, including resuscitation with intravenous fluids and vasopressors, respiratory support (e.g., supplemental oxygen, noninvasive ventilation, endotracheal intubation), antipyretics and analgesics, and hemorrhage control as needed. Mechanical ventilation, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and hemodialysis may be necessary. Conclusion Hantavirus may initially present with a non-specific viral prodrome, but travel and social history should prompt greater diagnostic suspicion. Patients are managed similarly to those with other viral hemorrhagic fevers.

analysis.background: Recent cases of Andes virus (ANDV) on a cruise ship in 2026 have highlighted the need for emergency clinicians to recognize hantavirus infection.
analysis.main_directions: The review covers hantavirus transmission via aerosolized rodent excreta, endothelial targeting leading to hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome or pulmonary syndrome, diagnostic ELISA testing, and supportive management including ventilation and hemodialysis.
analysis.current_state: Human hantavirus infection is known to arise from rodent exposure, causes distinct renal or pulmonary syndromes through endothelial injury, is diagnosed by IgG/IgM ELISA, and is managed primarily with supportive care.
analysis.gaps: The recent outbreak demonstrating possible human‑to‑human transmission of ANDV suggests limited data on transmissibility and infection control effectiveness.
analysis.future_research: Further studies should clarify the incubation period variability and factors influencing transmission to inform isolation guidelines and preventive strategies.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Recent cruise‑ship cases of Andes virus underscore the need for emergency clinicians to recognize hantavirus. Main directions: The review discusses rodent‑borne transmission, endothelial injury causing renal or pulmonary syndromes, ELISA diagnosis, and supportive care. Current state: Transmission, pathogenesis, diagnostic serology, and supportive treatment are well established. Gaps: Human‑to‑human transmission evidence is limited, raising infection‑control uncertainties. Future research: Studies on incubation period variability and transmission dynamics are needed to refine isolation and prevention.

papers.title: Omics Approaches in Hantavirus Research: Current Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are zoonotic RNA viruses responsible for two severe human diseases: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). Worldwide case fatality rates vary from 1% to 40%. Although single-layer genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics studies have advanced our understanding of hantavirus biology, true multi-omics integration remains scarce, leaving systems-level mechanisms of disease severity and host-pathogen interactions unresolved. High-throughput omics technologies have greatly advanced the study of hantavirus-host interactions. This review summarizes genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and AI-enabled approaches in hantavirus research. Genomic studies have clarified viral diversity, evolution, and reassortment, while transcriptomics has identified regulatory networks governing endothelial and innate immune responses. Proteomics has revealed host proteins involved in immune regulation, endothelial dysfunction, and potential therapeutic targeting, whereas metabolomics indicates substantial metabolic reprogramming during infection, although dedicated studies remain limited. AI-based approaches are increasingly applied to outbreak prediction, surveillance, and risk modeling. Drawing on successful multi-omics frameworks developed for other viral infections, we discuss opportunities to improve biomarker discovery, surveillance, therapeutic development, and future precision medicine strategies for hantavirus infections.

papers.title_zh: 关于汉坦病毒研究的组学方法:最新进展、挑战与未来展望。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 是人畜共患的 RNA 病毒,导致 肾综合征出血热 和 汉坦病毒心肺综合征,全球致死率范围为 1% 至 40%。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述概述了基因组学、转录组学、蛋白质组学、代谢组学以及人工智能驱动的方法在 汉坦病毒 研究中的应用。
analysis_zh.current_state: 高通量组学技术显著推动了对 汉坦病毒‐宿主相互作用的认识,揭示了病毒多样性、宿主调控网络以及免疫相关蛋白。

analysis_zh.future_research: 作者建议利用多组学框架和人工智能提升生物标志物发现、监测、治疗研发以及针对 汉坦病毒 感染的精准医学策略。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：汉坦病毒 是人畜共患的 RNA 病毒,导致 肾综合征出血热 和 汉坦病毒心肺综合征,全球致死率范围为 1% 至 40%。 主要方向：本综述概述了基因组学、转录组学、蛋白质组学、代谢组学以及人工智能驱动的方法在 汉坦病毒 研究中的应用。 研究现状：高通量组学技术显著推动了对 汉坦病毒‐宿主相互作用的认识,揭示了病毒多样性、宿主调控网络以及免疫相关蛋白。 不足：综合多组学分析仍然稀缺,导致疾病严重程度及宿主‐病原体动态的系统层面机制尚未阐明,且代谢组学研究有限。 后续研究：作者建议利用多组学框架和人工智能提升生物标志物发现、监测、治疗研发以及针对 汉坦病毒 感染的精准医学策略。

papers.title: Andes virus and sin nombre virus: Similarities and distinctive features.
papers.abstract: The threat of hanta virus infection has come to the forefront in recent weeks, following the outbreak of the Andes virus aboard the Dutch-flagged MV Hondius cruise ship during its spring 2026 voyage. Several passengers and crew members got infected because Andes virus is the sole known hanta virus to trigger human-to-human infection. All exposed passengers have returned to their countries in Asia, the Americas and Europe, and remain in quarantine to this day because of Andes virus extended incubation period (35-45 days). Several infected patients have died due to Andes high mortality (35-50%). Taken together, the unfolding of these alarming facts has ignited fears of a new hanta virus pandemic. Here, we briefly outline certain among the major similarities and distinctive features between Andes virus and Sin Nombre virus, the two principal hanta viruses known today to infect humans. This writing emphasizes how timely and critical it is to develop concerted research and accelerated testing programs for anti-hanta virus vaccines and antivirals.
